Jest is great for functions and APIs, but it cannot verify full user flows like “click a button → navigate → map loads → modal appears.” In our Next.js project, we built a Playwright E2E setup with three desktop browsers + two mobile viewports, organized by Desktop / Mobile directories. This post is a retrospective, not a rewrite of the official docs.
Why Playwright Compared with tools like Cypress, Playwright fit our needs especially well:
Native multi-browser support: one API for Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit Mobile emulation: built-in device presets like Pixel 5 and iPhone 12 Auth state reuse: log in once with storageState, reuse everywhere Works well with Next.js: webServer can start the dev server automatically; you can also run npm run dev first to speed things up Jest still handles unit and integration tests; Playwright covers frontend user flows.
Project Structure The core idea: layer by layout, split by page, extract shared logic into helpers.
tests/e2e/ ├── auth.setup.js # Log in once, save cookies ├── authentication.spec.js # Login flow itself (separate project) ├── helpers/ │ ├── pageHelpers.js # Shared: skip tour, suppress banners, wait for home │ ├── mapHelpers.js # Desktop map interactions │ └── detailHelpers.js ├── desktop/ │ ├── homePage.spec.js │ ├── detailsPage.spec.js │ └── searchPage.js └── mobile/ ├── homePage.spec.js ├── mobileTabBar.spec.js └── objsPage2/ └── objsPage2.map.spec.js Naming rule: **/*.spec.js. Desktop and Mobile run separately—avoid if (isMobile) branches inside one file.
Configuration: Projects for Multi-Browser + Layering playwright.config.ts is the backbone of the whole setup:
import { defineConfig, devices } from "@playwright/test"; import dotenv from "dotenv"; dotenv.config(); export default defineConfig({ testDir: "./tests", timeout: 90 * 1000, expect: { timeout: 45 * 1000 }, fullyParallel: false, retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0, workers: 2, reporter: "html", use: { baseURL: "http://localhost:3000", actionTimeout: 15 * 1000, navigationTimeout: 30 * 1000, trace: "on-first-retry", }, projects: [ // 1. Run setup first to generate auth state { name: "setup", testMatch: /auth\.setup\.js/, }, // 2. Test login flow separately (no storageState) { name: "authentication", testMatch: /authentication\.spec\.js/, use: { ...devices["Desktop Chrome"] }, }, // 3. Desktop × three browsers { name: "chromium", testMatch: /desktop\/.*\.spec\.(js|ts)/, use: { ...devices["Desktop Chrome"], storageState: "playwright/.auth/user.json", }, dependencies: ["setup"], }, { name: "firefox", testMatch: /desktop\/.*\.spec\.(js|ts)/, use: { ...devices["Desktop Firefox"], storageState: "playwright/.auth/user.json", }, dependencies: ["setup"], }, { name: "webkit", testMatch: /desktop\/.*\.spec\.(js|ts)/, use: { ...devices["Desktop Safari"], storageState: "playwright/.auth/user.json", }, dependencies: ["setup"], }, // 4. Mobile × two devices { name: "Mobile Chrome", testMatch: /mobile\/.*\.spec\.(js|ts)/, use: { ...devices["Pixel 5"], storageState: "playwright/.auth/user.json", }, dependencies: ["setup"], }, { name: "Mobile Safari", testMatch: /mobile\/.*\.spec\.(js|ts)/, use: { ...devices["iPhone 12"], storageState: "playwright/.auth/user.json", }, dependencies: ["setup"], }, ], webServer: { command: "npm run dev", url: "http://localhost:3000", reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI, timeout: 180 * 1000, }, }); Key design decisions:
Decision Reason testMatch by desktop/mobile path No viewport checks in every test dependencies: ["setup"] Ensures login runs before business tests fullyParallel: false Avoids parallel conflicts for write-heavy or shared-data tests reuseExistingServer: true (local) Skips startup wait when dev server is already running Global timeout 90s Google Maps and Auth0 redirects are slow Auth0 Login: setup + storageState Running through Auth0 on every test is too slow. Use a setup project to log in once and save cookies:
// tests/e2e/auth.setup.js const { test: setup, expect } = require("@playwright/test"); const authFile = "playwright/.auth/user.json"; setup("authenticate", async ({ page }) => { await page.goto("/"); await page.getByText("Sign In").click(); await page.waitForURL(/.*auth0.com/); await page.locator('input[name="username"]').fill(process.env.AUTH0_USERNAME); await page.locator('input[name="password"]').fill(process.env.AUTH0_PASSWORD); await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Continue" }).click(); await page.waitForURL(/localhost:3000/); await page.context().storageState({ path: authFile }); }); Put test credentials in .env:
AUTH0_USERNAME=test@example.com AUTH0_PASSWORD=your_test_password For anonymous tests, explicitly clear auth state:
test.describe("Unlogged", () => { test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] }, }); // ... }); Keep the login flow itself in authentication.spec.js, under its own project, separate from business tests.
Desktop / Mobile: What to Test and How to Split Rule: test shared components once; split forked UI Mobile and Desktop often share low-level components (e.g. Card), but the interaction shell differs:
Desktop map: marker click → overlay Mobile map: marker click → bottom SlideUpPanel Buttons triggered by hover on Desktop must be directly visible and tappable on Mobile—do not rely on .hover().
Mobile-specific locators Mobile often has duplicate DOM nodes where only one is visible. Plain getByTestId may match a hidden node:
const mobileHomeTab = (page, id) => page.locator(`#${id}`).filter({ visible: true }).first(); const visibleSharePanel = (page) => page.locator("#share-your-experience").locator("visible=true").first(); Helper Layer: Centralize Stability Logic Test files should read like user stories. Waiting, retries, and dialog suppression belong in helpers.
Shared helper (pageHelpers.js) async function suppressBannerDialogs(page) { await page.addInitScript(() => { localStorage.setItem("locationPermission", "denied"); localStorage.setItem("myapp_cookie_consent", "declined"); }); } Notes:
Use addInitScript to write localStorage before the page loads—more reliable than closing banners after load Use isVisible() instead of hard waits so missing tours do not cause timeouts Cross-browser navigation retry (mapHelpers.js) Firefox and WebKit often throw NS_BINDING_ABORTED during client-side routing races; Chromium usually does not:
export async function gotoStable(page, url, retries = 3) { for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) { try { await page.goto(url); return; } catch (err) { const isAbort = /NS_BINDING_ABORTED|interrupted by another navigation|frame was detached/i.test( err?.message ?? "" ); if (!isAbort || attempt >= retries) throw err; await page.waitForLoadState("load").catch(() => {}); } } } Issues that only appear in one browser are worth encoding in helpers with comments—future you will thank you.
Helpers by domain Helper Responsibility pageHelpers Home load, skip tour, suppress banners mapHelpers Desktop map markers, card menus, filters mobileMapHelpers Mobile bottom sheet, tap interactions How to Write Test Files 1. Split anonymous vs logged-in with describe test.describe("Unlogged", () => { test.use({ storageState: { cookies: [], origins: [] } }); // Public pages, cookie banner, footer }); test.describe("Logged In", () => { test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => { await page.goto("/"); await skipTourIfVisible(page); }); // Features that require login }); 2. Use serial mode for dependent flows Create → edit → delete chains:
test.describe("Logged In Map View", () => { test.describe.configure({ mode: "serial", timeout: 90000 }); // Firefox login + Google Maps init can exceed 60s }); 3. Prefer role / testid over fragile CSS // Good await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Delete" }).click(); await page.getByTestId("footer").toBeVisible(); // Third-party map components may require class selectors await page.locator(".gm-style").toBeVisible(); Add data-testid on critical interactions during development—E2E gets much more stable.
4. Skip when data is missing, do not hard-fail test.skip((await link.count()) === 0, `Top Contents don't have ${type}`); When test data is unstable, skip beats a wall of red.
Multi-Browser Lessons Learned In practice, the three browsers diverged more than expected:
Issue Symptom Fix Firefox slowness Maps init + login setup exceeds 60s Local timeout: 90000 WebKit navigation race page.goto aborted by client routing gotoStable retry Google Maps markers Click timing varies by engine dispatchEvent("click") + retry loop Hidden DOM nodes Mobile duplicate markup, multiple getByText matches .filter({ visible: true }) Third-party iframe Maps lives inside iframe Stable outer anchors like .gm-style Bottom line: passing in Chromium does not mean passing everywhere. In CI, run at least Firefox or WebKit alongside Chromium.
How to Run # Full suite (start dev server manually first for speed) npm run test:e2e # UI mode for debugging npm run test:e2e:ui # Desktop Chromium only npx playwright test --project=chromium # Mobile only npx playwright test --project="Mobile Chrome" # Single file npx playwright test tests/e2e/desktop/homePage.spec.js # View report npm run test:e2e:report Local tip: start the dev server first, then run tests. With reuseExistingServer: true, Playwright reuses the running server and avoids waiting for webServer startup.
Closing Thoughts Playwright’s value is not just “automating clicks”—it is keeping test cost under control through project structure:
Projects manage the browser and device matrix Directory layering handles Desktop / Mobile differences setup + storageState handles Auth0 login helpers handle stability and cross-browser patches Going from a few scattered specs to 30+ files covering home, map, details, editing, and search was not about writing more assertions—it was about getting layering and reuse right first. If you are on Next.js with third-party auth and a responsive dual-layout UI, this structure is ready to copy.

When you ship a web app, getting features working is only half the job. The other half is making sure search engines can find your site and understand each page correctly. This post walks through SEO for the Next.js App Router, based on a real project refactor: what SEO is, why it matters, what to configure, and how to manage it after launch.
What Is SEO? SEO (Search Engine Optimization) is a set of technical and content practices aimed at helping your site appear in organic search results on Google, Bing, and similar engines.
Search engines roughly follow three steps:
Crawl – bots visit your URLs Index – they analyze page content and store it Rank – they return relevant results when users search SEO is not about tricking algorithms. It is about helping crawlers understand your pages: title, description, canonical URL, and which pages should not be indexed.
For Next.js projects, SEO mostly lives in:
Meta tags in the HTML <head> Structured data (JSON-LD) robots.txt and sitemap.xml URL structure, canonical URLs, and redirects Blocking non-production environments from indexing Why Bother With SEO? 1. Organic traffic compounds over time Paid ads stop when you stop paying. Properly indexed pages can keep bringing visitors with very low marginal cost.
2. Dynamic content sites need it most User-generated routes, posts, events, and profile pages are all potential entry points. Without generateMetadata, a sitemap, and structured data, crawlers often only see the same empty HTML shell.
3. Social sharing uses the same meta tags WeChat, Twitter, Facebook, and Pinterest read Open Graph and Twitter Card tags when building link previews. SEO and share previews usually share one configuration.
4. Avoid “we launched but Google can’t find us” Common causes:
Staging environments getting indexed Login walls blocking crawlers No sitemap Duplicate URLs without a canonical All of these can be handled systematically in Next.js.
What to Configure in the Next.js App Router Below is a layered breakdown. Code uses generic examples you can drop into your own project.
1. Environment split: block indexing outside production If test or staging sites get indexed, they compete with production and may expose unreleased content.
Control this in the root layout via environment variables:
// app/layout.js const isProd = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL === "https://www.example.com"; export const metadata = { title: { default: "My App", template: "%s - My App", }, description: "Application description", openGraph: { type: "website", siteName: "My App", title: "My App", description: "Application description", images: [{ url: "/images/og-default.jpg", width: 1200, height: 630 }], }, // Non-production: site-wide noindex ...(!isProd && { robots: { index: false, follow: false } }), }; robots.js can add a second layer: non-production returns disallow: /:
// app/robots.js const BASE_URL = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL; const isProd = BASE_URL === "https://www.example.com"; export default function robots() { if (!isProd) { return { rules: [{ userAgent: "*", disallow: "/" }], }; } return { rules: [ { userAgent: "*", allow: "/", disallow: [ "/settings/", "/admin/", "/api/", // Edit pages, messages, etc. that require login ], }, ], sitemap: `${BASE_URL}/sitemap.xml`, }; } Key idea: allow public pages, disallow private ones. That is cleaner than opening everything and relying on per-page noindex alone.
2. Global metadata + per-page generateMetadata The App Router Metadata API is the recommended approach instead of manually editing <head>.
Root layout: site name, default title template, default OG image.
Individual pages: use generateMetadata for dynamic values. Detail pages read title, description, and cover image from the database:
// lib/generateDetailMetadata.js export async function generateDetailMetadata(id) { const item = await fetchItemById(id); if (!item) return {}; const slug = toSlug(item.displayName); const canonical = `${BASE_URL}/items/${id}${slug ? `/${slug}` : ""}`; const coverImage = item.imageUrl ?? null; return { title: item.displayName, description: item.description ?? "", alternates: { canonical }, openGraph: { url: canonical, title: item.displayName, description: item.description ?? "", images: coverImage ? [{ url: coverImage }] : [], }, twitter: { card: "summary_large_image", title: item.displayName, description: item.description ?? "", images: coverImage ? [coverImage] : [], }, }; } Use it in the page:
// app/items/[id]/[[...slug]]/page.js export async function generateMetadata({ params }) { const { id } = await params; return generateDetailMetadata(id); } Static pages like the homepage can also export their own generateMetadata and set a canonical URL pointing to the root.
3. Semantic URLs: ID + slug Bare IDs (/items/abc123) are weak for SEO and readability. A common pattern:
/items/{id}/{slug} The slug comes from the title and is human-friendly. The ID remains the primary key, so renaming only requires updating the slug.
When the slug is missing, redirect to the slugged URL to avoid duplicate content:
export default async function ItemPage({ params }) { const { id, slug } = await params; const item = await fetchItemById(id); if (!item) notFound(); if (!slug) { redirect(`/items/${id}/${toSlug(item.displayName)}`); } return <ItemDetail item={item} />; } Every detail page’s alternates.canonical should point to the full URL including the slug.
4. Dynamic sitemap Next.js 13+ supports app/sitemap.js, which generates sitemap.xml at build or request time.
Combine static pages with dynamic database entries:
// app/sitemap.js export default async function sitemap() { if (!isProd) return []; const staticUrls = [ { url: BASE_URL, changeFrequency: "daily", priority: 1 }, { url: `${BASE_URL}/about`, changeFrequency: "monthly", priority: 0.5 }, { url: `${BASE_URL}/search`, changeFrequency: "daily", priority: 0.8 }, ]; const dynamicUrls = []; const items = await fetchAllPublicItems(); for (const item of items) { const slug = toSlug(item.displayName); dynamicUrls.push({ url: `${BASE_URL}/items/${item._id}${slug ? `/${slug}` : ""}`, lastModified: item.updatedAt ?? new Date(), changeFrequency: "weekly", priority: 0.7, }); } return [...staticUrls, ...dynamicUrls]; } Notes:
Only include public pages that should be indexed Wrap per-collection fetches in try/catch so one failure does not break the entire sitemap Return [] outside production 5. Structured data (JSON-LD) Meta tags tell crawlers the title and summary. JSON-LD tells them what kind of entity the page represents.
Map content types to Schema.org types:
// lib/generateJsonLd.js export function generateJsonLd(item) { const url = `${BASE_URL}/items/${item._id}/${toSlug(item.displayName)}`; const base = { "@context": "https://schema.org", name: item.displayName, description: item.description, url, ...(item.image && { image: item.image }), }; switch (item.type) { case "attraction": return { ...base, "@type": "TouristAttraction" }; case "trip": return { ...base, "@type": "TouristTrip", startDate: item.startDate, endDate: item.endDate, }; case "article": return { ...base, "@type": "Article", datePublished: item.createdAt, dateModified: item.updatedAt, }; default: return null; } } Inject it in the page:
{ jsonLd && ( <script type="application/ld+json" dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(jsonLd) }} /> ); } After launch, validate with Google’s Rich Results Test.
6. Control indexing by permission On UGC sites, not every user profile should reach Google. Apply business rules:
const isIndexable = item.permission === "public" && item.status === "approved"; return { title: item.displayName, description: item.description, alternates: { canonical }, ...(!isIndexable && { robots: { index: false, follow: false } }), }; For private, draft, or unapproved content: exclude from the sitemap and set noindex. That is easier than cleaning up URLs in GSC later.
7. Middleware: don’t let login walls block social crawlers With Auth0 or similar middleware, Facebook and Pinterest bots fetching OG previews may get blocked too.
Allow known crawler user agents through (they still get SSR; only auth checks are skipped):
// middleware.ts const isSocialBot = userAgent.includes("facebookexternalhit") || userAgent.includes("Pinterestbot"); if (isSocialBot) { return NextResponse.next(); } Also exclude sitemap.xml and robots.txt from middleware:
export const config = { matcher: [ "/((?!_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)", ], }; 8. Other Next.js-related items Item Purpose manifest.json PWA / mobile experience; indirectly affects UX signals Default OG image 1200×630 Fallback when a page has no cover image viewport / themeColor Basic mobile experience Server-rendered detail pages Crawlers get full HTML immediately (App Router Server Components fit well) Analytics (GA4, Meta Pixel, etc.) do not directly equal SEO, but pairing GSC with GA is useful for comparing traffic and index status. Worth setting up alongside SEO.
Google Search Console Setup Once the code is in place, use GSC to prove site ownership and monitor indexing.
1. Add a property Open Google Search Console Add a property using Domain or URL prefix Domain: DNS verification; covers all subdomains and protocols URL prefix: verifies a single prefix, e.g. https://www.example.com 2. Ownership verification (three common methods) DNS TXT (domain verification, recommended)
Add the TXT record Google provides to your DNS. One verification covers the whole domain.
HTML file
Place googleXXXX.html in public/ and visit https://www.example.com/googleXXXX.html after deploy.
HTML meta tag
// app/layout.js export const metadata = { verification: { google: "your-verification-code", }, }; The Next.js Metadata API supports this natively—no manual <meta> tag needed.
3. Submit your sitemap After verification: Indexing → Sitemaps → Add https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml.
Within a few days, check discovered vs. indexed counts to confirm dynamic pages are being picked up.
4. What to monitor regularly Pages → Indexing: indexed, excluded, and error counts Experience → Core Web Vitals: LCP, CLS, etc. Links: external and internal link overview URL Inspection: whether a single URL is indexable and which canonical Google chose For new sites or large batches of new URLs, use URL Inspection → Request indexing to speed up initial discovery. You do not need to do this for every URL.
5. Other platforms (optional) Bing Webmaster Tools: can import GSC data Pinterest and others: sometimes require a verification HTML file or meta tag in public/, similar to GSC Post-mortem: a few things worth adding 1. Draw the indexing boundary first Decide what should be searchable: public detail pages, listings, about page. What should not: settings, admin, editors, DMs.
Map that to robots.js, sitemap.js, and per-page robots meta so nothing slips through.
2. Canonical URLs are first-class Query strings, missing slugs, and legacy path redirects should all resolve to one canonical URL. Otherwise GSC will report “Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user.”
3. Environment variables are your SEO switch Use NEXT_PUBLIC_BASE_URL to distinguish production from test. It is more reliable than NODE_ENV alone—some staging environments also run production builds.
4. A sitemap is a suggestion, not a guarantee Pages still need to be crawlable, have real content, not be noindexed, and load correctly. Meta tags, JSON-LD, and canonical URLs remain essential.
5. Test social previews separately Run URLs through the Facebook Sharing Debugger and Twitter Card Validator to confirm OG images and descriptions.
6. Performance is an SEO factor Core Web Vitals affect rankings. On the Next.js side: next/image, font optimization, and avoiding unnecessary large client bundles on detail pages.
7. Internationalization (if applicable) Use alternates.languages for hreflang tags to reduce duplicate-content issues across locales.
Minimal checklist Before launch, walk through this list:
Production root layout is not accidentally noindexed Staging / preview environments are noindexed and disallowed in robots robots.txt allows public pages and blocks private paths sitemap.xml includes static pages and indexable dynamic pages Detail pages have unique title, description, and canonical OG + Twitter Card are configured with a default fallback image Important content types have JSON-LD URLs include slugs; missing slugs 301 to the slugged URL Private content is noindexed and excluded from the sitemap Middleware does not block sitemap, robots, or social crawlers GSC is verified and the sitemap is submitted Rich Results Test and social sharing debuggers pass Closing thoughts The core idea of SEO in Next.js is simple: give crawlers the same clear, structured page information that users see, directly in server-rendered HTML.
The App Router’s metadata, generateMetadata, sitemap.js, and robots.js already standardize most of the plumbing. What actually separates good implementations is business logic: which pages to index, how to set canonicals, how dynamic data enters the sitemap, and how auth does not block crawlers.
Draw the boundary clearly, then ship against the checklist. That beats keyword stuffing every time.

content:
Our Original Architecture Early on, the project used a frontend database + backend sync model.
When a user opened the site, data was synced from the backend into a local browser database (IndexedDB / Dexie). After that, almost every read on the page went through this local layer instead of hitting the API on each navigation.
The upside was clear: the first load was slow, but everything after that felt very fast. Lists, detail views, filters, and sorting were essentially local reads with almost no network latency—closer to an offline-first web app than a classic SPA.
The downside was just as clear: it was bad for SEO.
Crawlers and social preview bots do not wait for your local sync to finish. They see the initial HTML and JS, not what lives in IndexedDB. Detail page titles, descriptions, and body content showed up empty—or as a generic shell—in search results and Facebook link previews. URLs were often query-based or routed through a single “details” path, which made independent, indexable, shareable pages hard to build.
The product worked. Discoverability did not. That gap is why we eventually moved toward SSR.
Why We Did Not Rewrite Everything at Once The frontend-database architecture already powered a large share of pages and components. A full, all-at-once SSR rewrite would have been high risk: huge scope, hard regression testing, and a real chance that TTFB would get worse everywhere.
What we actually did was incremental migration:
Start with pages: entry points that get shared and searched—detail pages, home, profile, about/legal—became Server Components that fetch primary data on the server Leave components alone for now: many child components still fetch secondary data with useEffect, close to the old pattern, keeping the change surface manageable Evolve the data layer in parallel: SSR requires the server to query the DB or call APIs directly; the local database slowly stepped back from “single source of truth” to optional or removed This was not “SSR good, CSR bad.” It was about moving what must be visible to the outside world onto server-rendered HTML without breaking the product.
How We Split Responsibilities During Migration Pages: SSR for what must appear in the first screen Core detail objects, initial home content, the main profile document, 404 handling, and permission checks—all of these need to exist in the HTML. Without that, SEO, link previews, and correct HTTP semantics (404 vs 200) do not hold up.
We also used this moment to fix URLs: semantic paths, ID + slug, redirects from legacy routes—done together with SSR so we would not accumulate redirect debt later.
Components: keep useEffect, but be deliberate about what they fetch Child components did not all need to move to SSR. Comments, favorites, notification state, sidebar extras—many were never on the critical first-screen path. Client-side fetching there still made sense.
The catch: SSR on the page does not mean components can fetch freely. Reads from the local DB were nearly free; every useEffect after migration is a real network call. We had to be intentional—merge requests where possible, cache where it helps (e.g. SWR)—so we would not end up with “SSR made the page faster, but a waterfall of API calls made the experience slower.”
Performance: SSR is not a free lunch The old model was slow once, then fast forever. SSR means every request can hit the server again. TTFB and database load need a fresh look.
In practice we traded on a few axes:
Primary data on the server, secondary data on the client—not one giant SSR payload Parallelize queries where it helps, but cap concurrency so connection pools do not get exhausted Do not block first HTML on non-critical data—ship the page, let components fill in Public pages like home can use revalidation to reduce cost per hit Guards and redirects on the server—less “flash the wrong page, then redirect” on the client The question shifted from “how do we make local reads faster?” to “what does the server render, what does the client add, and what does each path cost?”
Decoupling From the Frontend Database Was Part of the Same Effort Once pages SSR, Server Components cannot read IndexedDB. The old flow—open site → sync to local → pages read local—no longer works for public and SEO-sensitive routes.
In parallel we moved reads and writes toward backend APIs and shrank the local DB’s role. If you only change rendering and not data entry points, you fight the Server/Client boundary constantly—the server fetches one way, the client still reads locally, and inconsistencies follow.
Rough order: SSR public pages → move their read paths to APIs → leave editor/admin flows for later. You do not need full API coverage before the first SSR page, but both tracks should be planned together.
Lessons Learned (With the Old Architecture in Mind) Assuming SSR fixes all slowness—before, pain was first sync; after, pain is server queries and API waterfalls. The bottleneck moves; you have to measure again.
Page is SSR, components still fire many APIs—reads that were invisible with a local DB become N HTTP requests. First paint can feel worse unless you batch, cache, and lazy-load.
Mixing SEO pages and editor flows on one data path—public pages need a server-trustworthy source; editor pages can stay client-heavy, but the boundary must be explicit.
Handling slug, permissions, and 404 on the client—with a local DB, “no data yet” often meant an empty UI; for SEO routes, the server should own notFound, redirects, and canonical URLs.
First load vs every load—the old stack traded cold start for hot-path speed; SSR improves visibility but may add network round trips on each visit. The product has to accept that trade-off. You cannot expect “SEO-grade pages that feel exactly like a local database on every click.”
Relationship to SEO Work SSR is a prerequisite for SEO, not a substitute. Sitemaps, robots, metadata, and JSON-LD can come later—but if content still depends on the client and local storage, those tools only help so much.
Our sequence was: make searchable, shareable pages render content and meta on the server first, then add sitemap rules, indexing policy, and Search Console. Otherwise you end up tuning SEO on empty shells.
If Your Stack Looks Similar, Suggested Priorities Decide which pages must SSR—details, home, public profiles; not the whole site Change URLs together with SSR—one pass beats years of redirects SSR pages + useEffect components can coexist—reasonable, but cap component request volume Plan API migration alongside page migration—API-ization supports SSR; treat it as coupled work Set a performance budget separately—TTFB, API count, DB concurrency; do not judge the new stack with the old local-DB expectations Closing Thoughts Our migration was not from “pure CSR” to “pure SSR.” It was from a frontend-database-driven in-app experience to a hybrid model: public pages visible on the server, interactive pages still supplemented on the client.
The old approach traded first sync for later speed—a good deal inside the product, a bad deal for SEO. The new approach trades server-rendered first screens for discoverability, at the cost of redesigning data paths and request strategy.
If you started with local DB + sync, that is not a mistake. It still works well for tool-like, logged-in products. But pages that need to be found and shared eventually have to serve real content from the server. Replacing pages incrementally, leaving components on useEffect for now, and optimizing APIs and requests in parallel is a steady path forward.

Our Original Architecture

Early on, the project used a frontend database + backend sync model.

When a user opened the site, data was synced from the backend into a local browser database (IndexedDB / Dexie). After that, almost every read on the page went through this local layer instead of hitting the API on each navigation.

The upside was clear: the first load was slow, but everything after that felt very fast. Lists, detail views, filters, and sorting were essentially local reads with almost no network latency—closer to an offline-first web app than a classic SPA.
title: From a Frontend Database Architecture to Gradual SSR Migration

Background Some time ago, my boss told me that our web project needed to support offline usage — allowing users to use certain features even when they’re not connected to the internet. At first, I thought this was kind of magical. Normally, when a webpage can’t connect to the server, it just shows a 404 error, right?
After looking it up online, I learned about something called Service Worker, which can cache webpages so that when offline, the previously cached pages can still be used. At the same time, this technology also allows a website to work like an app: users can add the site to their phone’s home screen and open it just like an app. This is called PWA.
PWA PWA (Progressive Web App) is a technology that enables a website to feel like a native app.
In essence, it’s an “upgraded version of a website” that gives your site the following capabilities:
Can be installed on the phone’s home screen and opened like an app
Supports offline access (usable even without internet for some features)
Supports push notifications
Starts quickly and offers an experience close to native apps
Supports full-screen, splash screen, icons, and more
The core technology behind PWA is the Service Worker:
A Service Worker is a background JavaScript script in the browser that can intercept network requests from the webpage.
It can cache static resources (HTML, JS, CSS, images, etc.) locally.
When the user is offline, the Service Worker responds with cached content, enabling offline access.
Advantages of PWA:
Cross-platform: One codebase works on PC, Android, and iOS — no need to write separate native apps for each platform.
No app store required: users can access directly through the browser.
Auto-updating: Every time a new version is deployed, users get it automatically on their next visit.
How to use it My website is built with Next.js, so I checked the Next.js documentation and searched npm to see what packages were available. For Next.js, there’s a package called serwist/next, one of the earlier ones supporting PWA. There are also forks like @ducanh2912/next-pwa ，next-pwa . I decided to use @ducanh2912/next-pwa .
After installing the package, you only need to configure a few required files to get it working. I won’t go into the installation details here, but I’ll highlight a few important things.
The most important file is the manifest file, which works like an app’s app.json. It defines the app name, description, sizes, theme colors, display mode, and more.
Here’s an example:
{ "name": "PWA App", "short_name": "App", "icons": [ { "src": "/icons/android-chrome-192x192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png", "purpose": "any maskable" }, { "src": "/icons/android-chrome-384x384.png", "sizes": "384x384", "type": "image/png" }, { "src": "/icons/icon-512x512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" } ], "theme_color": "#FFFFFF", "background_color": "#FFFFFF", "start_url": "/", "display": "standalone", "orientation": "portrait" } The second one is to add metadata in app/layout.tsx or pages/_app.tsx. Here’s an example.
import type { Metadata, Viewport } from "next"; const APP_NAME = "PWA App"; const APP_DEFAULT_TITLE = "My Awesome PWA App"; const APP_TITLE_TEMPLATE = "%s - PWA App"; const APP_DESCRIPTION = "Best PWA app in the world!"; export const metadata: Metadata = { applicationName: APP_NAME, title: { default: APP_DEFAULT_TITLE, template: APP_TITLE_TEMPLATE, }, description: APP_DESCRIPTION, manifest: "/manifest.json", appleWebApp: { capable: true, statusBarStyle: "default", title: APP_DEFAULT_TITLE, // startUpImage: [], }, formatDetection: { telephone: false, }, openGraph: { type: "website", siteName: APP_NAME, title: { default: APP_DEFAULT_TITLE, template: APP_TITLE_TEMPLATE, }, description: APP_DESCRIPTION, }, twitter: { card: "summary", title: { default: APP_DEFAULT_TITLE, template: APP_TITLE_TEMPLATE, }, description: APP_DESCRIPTION, }, }; export const viewport: Viewport = { themeColor: "#FFFFFF", }; You can also set some other things here, for example making the iPhone status bar transparent so that content can be displayed inside the status bar.
Offline functionality To enable offline use, you need to configure Runtime caching. next-pwa comes with some custom caching configurations, but you can configure it as you like. For example, I’ve included the web pages that I want cached, and also the addresses of some image servers. This way, when users are offline, they can still see the images that were cached earlier while they were online.
const withPWA = require("@ducanh2912/next-pwa").default({ // Your other options, extendDefaultRuntimeCaching: true, workboxOptions: { runtimeCaching: [ // Your runtimeCaching array ], }, }); module.exports = withPWA({ // Your Next.js config }); Add Website to Home Screen For iPhone, just open the page in Safari, then select “Add to Home Screen” from the menu. For Android devices, after selecting “Add to Home Screen”, there are two options: one is Install, and the other is Add Bookmark. To get an app-like experience, you should choose Install. This way, the website can be accessed on the phone just like a native app. Conclusion Overall, PWA really impressed me. After configuring it, I could use the website on my iPhone just like an app — without seeing the browser’s UI, the website itself takes up the entire screen. By adjusting the website’s responsive design and other settings, it’s fully possible to deliver an app-like experience while reducing development costs.
References Workbox | Chrome for Developers Serwist @ducanh2912/next-pwa next-pwa

Preface Since we hadn’t traveled far in quite a while, at the end of February, my girlfriend Chelsea, our friend Jennie, and I planned a trip to New Plymouth on New Zealand’s North Island.
I first noticed this place because of its beautiful snow-capped mountain. This time, our goal was to hike and see the mountain up close. If you check out this area on Google Maps Street View, you’ll notice a perfect circle of greenery — right at the center of that circle is our destination: Mt. Taranaki, often called the “Mt. Fuji of New Zealand.”
Day 1 We set off from Auckland in the morning, picked up Jennie, and started driving south along State Highway 1 — a journey that took about five hours in total. Chelsea took the first stretch from Auckland to Hamilton, getting some experience with long-distance driving. I took over for the rest of the way.
On the drive, we passed many charming small towns and vast farmlands, with rolling hills filled with sheep and cows, and tall, lush cornfields lining the roads.
We arrived in New Plymouth around 2 p.m. and had a tasty Vietnamese lunch. Our first stop was Cape Egmont Lighthouse. This white lighthouse stands between the green pastures and the rugged coastline, with the cloud-covered peak of Taranaki looming in the background. It felt like a silent guardian watching over the land. There were no crowds, just the sound of the wind and waves. The sunlight filtered through the clouds and lit up the lighthouse — as if time itself had slowed.
Back in town, we visited New Plymouth’s famous Coastal Walkway. We stopped at the well-known seaside railway crossing (like a mini version of Kamakura in Japan), then followed the walkway to the iconic Wind Wand — a red, bendy art installation dancing in the sea breeze. It represents the free, flowing, and artistic soul of the city.
Dinner was at a popular Thai restaurant. Unexpectedly, a group of elderly locals from a nearby retirement home were also dining there. After eating, they gathered together and sang a beautiful Māori song. It was the first full Māori-language song I’d heard since moving to New Zealand two years ago. Though I didn’t understand the lyrics, the harmonies and shared emotion moved me. One of the elders even came up afterward and asked why we hadn’t sung along — I told him I really wanted to, but sadly, I didn’t know the words.
Day 2 We started the day with breakfast at Elixir Café, a great spot with delicious brunch options — highly recommended! Then we headed out to Kent Road to find the famous photo spot with the road leading directly to Mt. Taranaki. Sadly, we struggled to find it at first and only located it after doubling back. Even then, the mountain was hidden behind clouds. We still didn’t realize how bad the visibility would get later…
Next up was the highlight of the trip: hiking around Mt. Taranaki. One famous photo spot on this trail features the mountain perfectly reflected in a small alpine pool. The trail itself is relatively flat but long — about 15km return and roughly 6 hours to complete.
After parking and a quick toilet break, we took a group photo and started the hike. Most of the trail winds through native forest, so it’s shaded and not too hot. The path is well maintained, flat, and easygoing — a truly pleasant walk.
Unfortunately, Jennie isn’t a regular hiker, and halfway through the hike, she was exhausted. We kept encouraging her, saying “Just around the next corner!” to keep her going — and to her credit, it worked. When we reached the ridge, light rain started falling. By the time we arrived at the reflection point, the entire area was engulfed in thick fog. Visibility dropped to less than 20 meters. We could barely see the water, let alone the mountain or its reflection. We asked two other hikers if they’d seen the mountain — they laughed and said, “Maybe it’s out there somewhere.”
We had a snack and began the return journey. Jennie, claiming her legs were “gone,” hobbled her way down. As we descended, the rain intensified. We went from light drizzle to steady rain, arriving back at the car drenched but laughing — a perfect “before and after” photo moment.
Back at the carpark, we chatted with a couple of hikers who were planning to stay overnight and return early for sunrise photos. We wished them the best of luck!
Exhausted, we headed back to our Airbnb to rest.
Day 3 The weather was finally clear, and Mt. Taranaki stood tall and proud — visible even from the road. We regretted not having this weather the day before, but made the most of it by heading to Te Rewa Rewa Bridge for some final mountain photos. It was our last planned day in New Plymouth, so we hit the road for our next destination: Skyline Rotorua, to ride the luge. Chelsea remembered it fondly from last time, and we thought it’d be a fun way to wrap up the trip. On the drive, Chelsea said three days wasn’t enough — so we decided to extend the trip by one more day.
But when we arrived at Skyline, the gondola was broken. With no estimate for when it would be fixed, we changed plans and went to soak at Polynesian Spa, Rotorua’s most famous geothermal hot spring. The ticket we bought gave us access to seven pools.
As we neared Rotorua, the smell of sulfur filled the air — the famous “rotten egg” aroma that comes with geothermal activity. At the spa, the scent was even stronger, but the warm pools made it all worth it.
For dinner, we went to Yamato Japanese Restaurant, where you sit around the kitchen and watch chefs prepare everything fresh — sashimi, sushi, and grilled meats. Everything was delicious and the experience was intimate and lively.
Day 4 This spontaneous extra day turned out to be a blast. We started the morning with breakfast from Rotorua’s most popular bakery, then headed to Agrodome Farm.
There, we watched a sheep show, hand-fed alpacas and sheep, tasted local honey, admired kiwi vines, and even saw a few deer!
Final Thoughts Four days and three nights — a trip filled with laughter, surprises, and unforgettable moments. Despite the rain, fog, and a broken gondola, we came away with so many great memories. From the elderly choir singing in Māori to alpacas chasing us for food, every moment was worth it.
Can’t wait for the next adventure.

1. Background When using the Google Maps JavaScript API, there may be scenarios where users need to query routes. In such cases, how can navigation routes be displayed on the map?
2. Related Concepts With the Google Directions API, you can retrieve navigation information between two or more locations — such as distance, duration, and route details on the map. By passing this data to the Maps JavaScript API, it’s possible to render the navigation route directly on an embedded map.
Before using Google Maps and the Directions API, you need to create a project in Google Cloud Platform, enable the corresponding APIs, and set up billing. Google Cloud Platform also offers a certain amount of free usage credits.
3. How to Display Navigation Routes There are two ways to implement this functionality.
A. Use the Built-in DirectionsRenderer from the Maps JavaScript API The Maps JavaScript API includes a built-in DirectionsRenderer feature, which allows you to retrieve and display navigation routes directly on the map. You can refer to the following example code:
//Assuming the Google Map object has already been initialized const map = new window.google.maps.Map(mapRef.current, mapOptions); //DirectionsService function calculateAndDisplayRoute() { const directionsService = new google.maps.DirectionsService(); const directionsRenderer = new google.maps.DirectionsRenderer({ suppressMarkers: true, // Hide default tags polylineOptions: { strokeColor: "#4285F4", strokeOpacity: 0.9, strokeWeight: 7, }, }); directionsRenderer.setMap(map); // Build the waypoints for the route (skip the first and last markers) const waypoints = objArray.slice(1, objArray.length - 1).map((marker) => ({ location: new google.maps.LatLng( marker.locationInfo.location.lat, marker.locationInfo.location.lng ), stopover: true, })); directionsService.route( { origin: new google.maps.LatLng( objArray[0].locationInfo.location.lat, objArray[0].locationInfo.location.lng ), // Start point destination: new google.maps.LatLng( objArray[objArray.length - 1].locationInfo.location.lat, objArray[objArray.length - 1].locationInfo.location.lng ), // End point waypoints: waypoints, // Midpoints travelMode: google.maps.TravelMode.DRIVING, // an use DRIVING, WALKING, BICYCLING, TRANSIT region: "NZ", language: "en", }, (response, status) => { if (status === "OK") { const navigation = { legs: response.routes[0].legs.map((leg) => ({ distance: leg.distance, duration: leg.duration, })), overviewPolyline: response.routes[0].overview_polyline, }; const path = google.maps.geometry.encoding.decodePath( navigation.overviewPolyline ); const polyline = new google.maps.Polyline({ path: path, geodesic: true, strokeColor: "#4285F4", // color strokeOpacity: 0.8, strokeWeight: 7, }); polyline.setMap(map); // directionsRenderer.setDirections(response); // Render the route on the map } else { console.error("Directions request failed due to " + status); } } ); } calculateAndDisplayRoute(); B. Use the Directions API to fetch route data You can retrieve navigation data for a specific route by querying the Google Directions API via the following endpoint: https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/directions/json const url = createUrl({ beginning: "https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/directions/json", searchParams: { ["origin"]: origin, ["destination"]: destination, ["waypoints"]: waypoints, ["mode"]: mode, // Can use DRIVING, WALKING, BICYCLING, TRANSIT ["region"]: "NZ", ["language"]: "en", ["key"]: apiKey, }, }); const response = await fetch(url); if (!response.ok) { const errorData = await response.json(); console.error("Error from Google Directions API:", errorData); return NextResponse.json( { message: "Failed to fetch directions", error: errorData }, { status: response.status } ); } const data = await response.json(); const navigation = { legs: data.routes[0].legs.map((leg) => ({ distance: leg.distance, duration: leg.duration, })), overviewPolyline: data.routes[0].overview_polyline.points, }; The legs field contains segment information. If you have multiple locations along the route, each segment will be stored as a separate leg.
The overview_polyline provides the encoded polyline used to display the entire route on the map.
When using the map, you can display the navigation route by passing the route data into the map. //Create a Map const map = new window.google.maps.Map(mapRef.current, mapOptions); //Use Ctrl to zoom map.setOptions({ gestureHandling: "cooperative", // Zoom in/out with Ctrl. }); //set Polyline route if (navigation.overviewPolyline) { const path = new google.maps.geometry.encoding.decodePath( navigation.overviewPolyline ); const polyline = new google.maps.Polyline({ path: path, geodesic: true, strokeColor: "#318156", // Google blue strokeOpacity: 0.9, strokeWeight: 6, }); polyline.setMap(map); } The result is shown in the cover image.
Summary Both methods can be used to load navigation routes, each suitable for different scenarios.
Method A is ideal for situations where you need to query and display routes in real-time. If you don’t need to fetch the route every time, you can use Method B, which involves calling the Directions API separately, storing the route data in a database, and then reading it when needed. This approach helps avoid repeated API calls and reduces usage costs.

1. Background Recently, I developed a full stack project with friends, including React front-end and Express back-end, stored in a GitHub repository. I want to launch and deploy this project now.
For React projects, there are many free deployment platforms, such as Vercel and DigitalOcean. But considering that this project includes both the front-end and back-end, consider deploying them in one place. After consulting many materials, it was decided to deploy this full stack project to the AWS cloud.
This article mainly introduces how to deploy a complete project on AWS EC2.
2. Create AWS EC2 instance Open EC2 Choose Launch Instance Select Ubuntu server in the image list and select free tier For Instance type, choose t2.micro Set key pair Network settings：because you want to access through the Internet, you need to allow http and https access The remaining configuration content will be configured according to your needs. Then click Launch instance to start instance. 3. Configure EC2 instance environment Connect to EC2 instanse（with user name root). After connecting, the Ubuntu terminal will open on a new webpage. Run the following command to update the Ubuntu server, close this webpage after completion, and then reconnect again
sudo apt-get update Run the following command to install the required software
sudo apt-get install curl //install curl curl -sL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_14.x | sudo -E bash - sudo apt-get install -y nodejs //install nodejs sudo npm install pm2@latest -g //install pm2 sudo apt-get install nginx -y //install nginx //Check the version of the installed software node -v npm -v nginx -v Configure security group Add a new rule, select Custom TCP, set the port to 3000, and set the source to Anywhere Add a new rule, select Custom TCP, set the port to 80, and set the source to Anywhere After completing the above steps, open the new tab using EC2’s Public IPv4 DNS or Public IPv4 address to see the welcome page template for nginx
4. Download the React project and run forever Because I have already completed the React project, I directly used Git to download the project
Download Git project
git clone https://github.com/your-username/your-project.git //Then use your username and token to log in Jump to the React project directory and then build the project. We need to confirm the name of the output file after compilation, which will be used later. The output folder in my project is ‘/dist ‘,
cd /projectname/ npm install npm run build Modify the nginx configuration file and start the project
Jump to the path of /etc/nginx and edit the nginx. conf file
Change user to root Add follow code in http section
server{ listen 80; server_name _; location /{ root /root/project-name/frontend/dist; //ouptut folder after build index index.html; //index file try_files $uri /index.html; } } Use the following command to check the nginx configuration, and then restart nginx
sudo nginx -t //check sudo systemctl restart nginx //Restart nginx sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/error.log //check error log At this point, the React project has been deployed and the previously opened public IP page can be refreshed to see if the webpage can be opened
5. Nodejs forever run My react and nodejs sections are in the same git repository, so I no longer need a clone. If in different git projects, please clone your nodejs project first.
Install the required software
npm install npm start Stop with Ctrl + C
Use pm2 to run the nodejs project
cd src //Jump to the nodejs project directory npm2 start app.js //Start the nodejs project //pm2 command pm2 list //View all processes pm2 log //View log pm2 delete all //Stop all processes At this point, the nodejs service has been started and can be tested by entering your API in your browser.
6. Notes If there is an environment variable in your project that records the address of localhost, remember to modify localhost or 127.0.0.1 to the current public DNS of EC2 If you have Google OAuth2.0, you need to add public DNS for EC2 in its settings to allow access.

<a href="{{ .Destination | safeURL }}"{{ with .Title}} title="{{ . }}"{{ end }}{{ if strings.HasPrefix .Destination "http" }} target="_blank" rel="noopener"{{ end }}>{{ .Text | safeHTML }}</a> All links within the article will be automatically added with target="_blank" rel="noopener"

After installing the theme, you can copy the files circled in the following image to the corresponding directory on the site, so that you can customize the style of the blog without affecting the update of the theme.

Hugo will prioritize reading files from the site directory when loading, and if not, read files from the theme directory.

  1. Replace the code in layouts/partials/toc.html with the following：
{{- $headers := findRE "<h[1-6].*?>(.|\n])+?</h[1-6]>" .Content -}}
{{- $has_headers := ge (len $headers) 1 -}}
{{- if $has_headers -}}
<aside id="toc-container" class="toc-container wide">
    <div class="toc">
        <details {{if (.Param "TocOpen") }} open{{ end }}>
            <summary accesskey="c" title="(Alt + C)">
                <span class="details">{{- i18n "toc" | default "Table of Contents" }}</span>
            </summary>

            <div class="inner">
                {{- $largest := 6 -}}
                {{- range $headers -}}
                {{- $headerLevel := index (findRE "[1-6]" . 1) 0 -}}
                {{- $headerLevel := len (seq $headerLevel) -}}
                {{- if lt $headerLevel $largest -}}
                {{- $largest = $headerLevel -}}
                {{- end -}}
                {{- end -}}

                {{- $firstHeaderLevel := len (seq (index (findRE "[1-6]" (index $headers 0) 1) 0)) -}}

                {{- $.Scratch.Set "bareul" slice -}}
                <ul>
                    {{- range seq (sub $firstHeaderLevel $largest) -}}
                    <ul>
                        {{- $.Scratch.Add "bareul" (sub (add $largest .) 1) -}}
                        {{- end -}}
                        {{- range $i, $header := $headers -}}
                        {{- $headerLevel := index (findRE "[1-6]" . 1) 0 -}}
                        {{- $headerLevel := len (seq $headerLevel) -}}

                        {{/* get id="xyz" */}}
                        {{- $id := index (findRE "(id=\"(.*?)\")" $header 9) 0 }}

                        {{- /* strip id="" to leave xyz, no way to get regex capturing groups in hugo */ -}}
                        {{- $cleanedID := replace (replace $id "id=\"" "") "\"" "" }}
                        {{- $header := replaceRE "<h[1-6].*?>((.|\n])+?)</h[1-6]>" "$1" $header -}}

                        {{- if ne $i 0 -}}
                        {{- $prevHeaderLevel := index (findRE "[1-6]" (index $headers (sub $i 1)) 1) 0 -}}
                        {{- $prevHeaderLevel := len (seq $prevHeaderLevel) -}}
                        {{- if gt $headerLevel $prevHeaderLevel -}}
                        {{- range seq $prevHeaderLevel (sub $headerLevel 1) -}}
                        <ul>
                            {{/* the first should not be recorded */}}
                            {{- if ne $prevHeaderLevel . -}}
                            {{- $.Scratch.Add "bareul" . -}}
                            {{- end -}}
                            {{- end -}}
                            {{- else -}}
                            </li>
                            {{- if lt $headerLevel $prevHeaderLevel -}}
                            {{- range seq (sub $prevHeaderLevel 1) -1 $headerLevel -}}
                            {{- if in ($.Scratch.Get "bareul") . -}}
                        </ul>
                        {{/* manually do pop item */}}
                        {{- $tmp := $.Scratch.Get "bareul" -}}
                        {{- $.Scratch.Delete "bareul" -}}
                        {{- $.Scratch.Set "bareul" slice}}
                        {{- range seq (sub (len $tmp) 1) -}}
                        {{- $.Scratch.Add "bareul" (index $tmp (sub . 1)) -}}
                        {{- end -}}
                        {{- else -}}
                    </ul>
                    </li>
                    {{- end -}}
                    {{- end -}}
                    {{- end -}}
                    {{- end }}
                    <li>
                        <a href="#{{- $cleanedID -}}" aria-label="{{- $header | plainify -}}">{{- $header | safeHTML -}}</a>
                        {{- else }}
                    <li>
                        <a href="#{{- $cleanedID -}}" aria-label="{{- $header | plainify -}}">{{- $header | safeHTML -}}</a>
                        {{- end -}}
                        {{- end -}}
                        <!-- {{- $firstHeaderLevel := len (seq (index (findRE "[1-6]" (index $headers 0) 1) 0)) -}} -->
                        {{- $firstHeaderLevel := $largest }}
                        {{- $lastHeaderLevel := len (seq (index (findRE "[1-6]" (index $headers (sub (len $headers) 1)) 1) 0)) }}
                    </li>
                    {{- range seq (sub $lastHeaderLevel $firstHeaderLevel) -}}
                    {{- if in ($.Scratch.Get "bareul") (add . $firstHeaderLevel) }}
                </ul>
                {{- else }}
                </ul>
                </li>
                {{- end -}}
                {{- end }}
                </ul>
            </div>
        </details>
    </div>
</aside>
<script>
    let activeElement;
    let elements;
    window.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function (event) {
        checkTocPosition();

        elements = document.querySelectorAll('h1[id],h2[id],h3[id],h4[id],h5[id],h6[id]');
        // Make the first header active
        activeElement = elements[0];
        const id = encodeURI(activeElement.getAttribute('id')).toLowerCase();
        document.querySelector(`.inner ul li a[href="#${id}"]`).classList.add('active');
    }, false);

    window.addEventListener('resize', function(event) {
        checkTocPosition();
    }, false);

    window.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
        // Check if there is an object in the top half of the screen or keep the last item active
        activeElement = Array.from(elements).find((element) => {
            if ((getOffsetTop(element) - window.pageYOffset) > 0 &&
                (getOffsetTop(element) - window.pageYOffset) < window.innerHeight/2) {
                return element;
            }
        }) || activeElement

        elements.forEach(element => {
            const id = encodeURI(element.getAttribute('id')).toLowerCase();
            if (element === activeElement){
                document.querySelector(`.inner ul li a[href="#${id}"]`).classList.add('active');
            } else {
                document.querySelector(`.inner ul li a[href="#${id}"]`).classList.remove('active');
            }
        })
    }, false);

    const main = parseInt(getComputedStyle(document.body).getPropertyValue('--article-width'), 10);
    const toc = parseInt(getComputedStyle(document.body).getPropertyValue('--toc-width'), 10);
    const gap = parseInt(getComputedStyle(document.body).getPropertyValue('--gap'), 10);

    function checkTocPosition() {
        const width = document.body.scrollWidth;

        if (width - main - (toc * 2) - (gap * 4) > 0) {
            document.getElementById("toc-container").classList.add("wide");
        } else {
            document.getElementById("toc-container").classList.remove("wide");
        }
    }

    function getOffsetTop(element) {
        if (!element.getClientRects().length) {
            return 0;
        }
        let rect = element.getBoundingClientRect();
        let win = element.ownerDocument.defaultView;
        return rect.top + win.pageYOffset;
    }
</script>

1. Introduction 1.1 What is Hugo Hugo is one of the most popular open-source static site generators. With its amazing speed and flexibility, Hugo makes building websites fun again.
1.2 What is Github Pages GitHub Pages is a static site hosting service that directly retrieves HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files from the repository on GitHub, (optional) runs the files through the build process, and then publishes the website.
Users can host sites on GitHub’s GitHub.io domain or their own custom domain.
Github Pages Doc 2. Preparation This tutorial assumes that you have already understood the basic usage of Git and Github. If you are not familiar, you can refer to Getting Git right 。
2.1 Environment You need to install the following environment:
Git Hugo IDEs that one is accustomed to using, such as VSCode 2.2 Install Hugo I am using a Windows 11 system, and the installation process is as follows:
Install Go language，Download - Go Download the archive of Hugo binary file，Hugo - latest release (This article was released on February 11, 2024. If there is a new version, please update it yourself) Extract the archive, move the executable to the desired directory. Add this directory to the PATH environment variable Open the PowerShell, run hugo version. If the version number is displayed, the installation is successful Hugo installation for other systems can refer to Hugo Installation 2.3 Setup Github repository Create two Github repositories, one for storing Hugo blog source code and one for storing static web pages generated by Hugo.
Create Github Pages repository
Name it like <username>.github.io, <username> is your Github username. This repository is used to store static web pages. Set to Public, otherwise it cannot be accessed through the browser. Check to add README file, which will set the main branch as the default main branch of the repository Create a blog source repository
Name it as you like, this repository is used to store the source code of the Hugo blog. Set it to Public or Private according to your needs. Clone the repository to your local machine as the working directory for creating the Hugo blog. 3. Create a blog with Hugo 3.1 Initialize a Hugo site In your cloned repository folder，open PowerShell and run hugo new site <site_name>，in which <site_name> is up to you to decide. For example:
hugo new site MyFreshWebsite --format yaml --format yaml It is specified that the configuration file format is in yaml format. I personally think this file format is more intuitive
After creation, generate 7 main folders and 1 file (there are added folders in the figure for reference only) archetypes: article templates content: store the content of the blog data: store data files layouts: store customized templates public: store the generated static web pages static: store static files such as images, CSS, and JavaScript themes: store the theme of the blog hugo.yml: the configuration file of the blog 3.2 hugo.yml configuration Open hugo.yml, modify the configuration according to your needs. The following is a simple example:
baseURL: "https://<yourname>.github.io/" # Your website URL languageCode: en-us title: <Your Nmae> # Your blog title theme: <theme_name> # The theme you want to use enableInlineShortcodes: true # Enable shortcodes enableEmoji: true # Enable emoji enableRobotsTXT: true # Enable robots.txt hasCJKLanguage: true # Enable CJK language support buildDrafts: false buildFuture: false buildExpired: false paginate: 15 # Number of articles per page minify: disableXML: true minifyOutput: true permalinks: # URL format post: "/:title/" defaultContentLanguage: en # Default language defaultContentLanguageInSubdir: true languages: en: languageName: "English" weight: 1 menu: main: - name: Articles url: posts/ weight: 1 - name: Tags url: tags/ weight: 10 - name: Search url: search/ weight: 11 zh: languageName: "中文" weight: 2 menu: main: - name: 文章 url: posts/ weight: 1 - name: 标签 url: tags/ weight: 10 - name: 搜索 url: search/ weight: 11 params: socialIcons: - name: github title: View Source on Github url: "https://github.com/ryanwooa" - name: Instagram url: "https://www.instagram.com/ryanwu5_/" - name: X url: "https://twitter.com/nzw897" - name: linkedin url: "https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryan-wu-9b8161268/" ShowBreadCrumbs: true ShowRelatedPosts: true ShowPostNavLinks: true ShowCodeCopyButtons: true ShowReadingTime: true label: icon: "q3.png" env: production author: Ryan Wu defaultTheme: auto disableThemeToggle: false DateFormat: "2006-01-02" ShowShareButtons: true ShowReadingTime: true # disableSpecialistPost: true displayFullLangName: true ShowPostNavLinks: true ShowBreadCrumbs: true ShowCodeCopyButtons: true hideFooter: false #hide footer ShowWordCounts: true VisitCount: true ShowLastMod: true #show last modified date ShowToc: true # show table of contents TocOpen: true # expand table of contents by default assets: favicon: "q3.png" favicon16x16: "q3.png" favicon32x32: "q3.png" apple_touch_icon: "q3.png" safari_pinned_tab: "q3.png" outputs: home: - HTML - RSS - JSON # necessary for search taxonomies: tag: tags category: categories 4. Install Hugo theme There are many themes to choose from in the Hugo theme , and you can choose a theme according to your preferences. Taking PaperMod as an example here.
According PaperMod Install/Update ，it can be installed using the following command：
git submodule add --depth=1 https://github.com/adityatelange/hugo-PaperMod.git themes/PaperMod git submodule update --init --recursive # needed when you reclone your repo (submodules may not get cloned automatically) Then you can see that the newly installed theme folder is added to the themes folder.
Configure it in hugo.yml file：
theme: PaperMod For more PaperMod function you can refer to PaperMod - Features 5. New post If you want to create a new article, you can use the following command to create a new Markdown file:
hugo new xxx.md hugo new posts/xxx.md # If you want to create a new article in the posts folder The Markdown file created by this command will automatically include some basic information, such as the article title, date, etc. You can edit the article content in the Markdown file.
draft = true shows that this article is currently a draft. If you want the article to be displayed on the website, you need to set draft to false or delete this line.
6. Preview and debug After creating the article, you can use the following command to preview the website locally:
hugo server Open your browser and navigate to http://localhost:1313
7. Deploy to Github Pages using Github Action GitHub Actions is a CI/CD platform that can be used to automatically execute build, test, and deployment pipelines. We can use Github Action to automatically deploy the Hugo blog to Github Pages.
7.1 Create Workflow In the root directory of the project, create a .github/workflows folder, and create a workflow file with a .yml extension. My GitHub Action automatically publishes the file main.yml example configuration is as follows:
name: GitHub Pages on: push: branches: - main pull_request: jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-22.04 concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: submodules: true fetch-depth: 0 - name: Setup Hugo uses: peaceiris/actions-hugo@v2 with: hugo-version: 'latest' extended: true # use Hugo extended version - name: Build run: hugo --minify - name: Deploy uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3 if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' with: personal_token: ${{ secrets.PERSONAL_BLOG}} # replace with your own token external_repository: ryanwooa/ryanwooa.github.io # replace with your own repository publish_dir: ./public #cname: www.example.com # custom domain secrets.PERSONAL_BLOG is a personal access token that is generated in the Settings->Developer settings->Personal access tokens of the personal account, and requires the repo and workflow permissions.
And you need to add the secrets in the repository settings: Settings->Secrets for automatic deployment of Hugo Blog to GitHub Pages.
After generating the token, you need to set secrets in the settings of the blog source repository and fill in the token value that was just generated. In this way, the ${secrets.PERSONAL_BLOG} in the action configuration file can obtain this value.
7.2 Publish to Github Pages After completing the above configuration, every time you modify the article locally, you only need to push the modification to the GitHub repository, and GitHub Action will deploy the web page generated by Hugo to the gh-pages branch of the Github Pages repository.
Set the deploy branch to gh-pages in the settings of the Github Pages repository, so you can access your blog through https://username.github.io.
8. Reference 如何用 GitHub Pages + Hugo 搭建个人博客 Hugo + GitHub Action，搭建你的博客自动发布系统 [置顶] hugo博客搭建 | PaperMod主题 Hugo Documentation Github Pages quickstart
